# Source-backed peerage identity design

Recommendation. Add a resolution-run alias context built solely from explicit source bridges. Keep syntax and title recognition in `funder_name`; keep cross-observation ambiguity and identity decisions in declaration resolution. Do not add columns or migrations.

## Grounding

`funder_name.rs` currently owns normalized punctuation-preserving personal names and the single `PersonTitle` vocabulary. `ParsedPersonName` strips recognized leading titles, and `unwrap_given_name` only handles a parenthesized given name before a surname. Consequently `Lord David Sainsbury of Turville` currently yields `david sainsbury of turville`, while the explicit `Baron ... (David Sainsbury)` bridge cannot establish identity.

`ResolutionInput::scoring_input` groups observations into unchanged name/address profiles and unions their blocking keys. `input.rs::blocking_keys` and `identity.rs::classify` both call `individual_donor_name`, whose gate requires donor role and person kind. Scored profile pairs expand back into observation pairs before classification. This is the seam for a shared, computed evidence index. Preserve original comparison names, score probabilities, profile grouping, budget checks, and company/person component restrictions.

## Caller sketch

At validated input construction, derive `PeerageAliases` once from all eligible observations. Both `blocking_keys` and `classify` consult the same per-observation evidence key. The index provides no key for unresolved or ambiguous names.

```rust
let peerage_aliases = PeerageAliases::from_observations(&observations);
// Existing exact person evidence remains independent.
if let Some(key) = input.peerage_aliases.personal_name(&observation.funder_id) {
    keys.insert(format!("peerage-person:{key}"));
}
let peerage_agrees = input.peerage_aliases.agree(&a.funder_id, &b.funder_id);
```

The ordinary personal-name observation must also receive the peerage key when its exact normalized name is one of the index's supported personal names. Otherwise blocking will miss the bridge-to-plain-name pair. `agree` must require two present keys, never `None == None`.

## Ownership and types

In `funder_name.rs`, use a private-field syntax model, for example `PeerageName` with `Style` and `ExplicitBridge` variants, plus exact normalized `PeerageStyle` and `PersonalName` values. The parser accepts raw source and applies the existing normalization. It does not resolve an identity. This can live in a child module if needed for file size, but the module is part of funder-name ownership rather than a competing title parser.

Extend `PersonTitle` with Baron, and any other consciously supported peerage titles, using its canonical `from_token` and an exhaustive title-category match. Do not create another string list of title variants. Avoid broadening titles beyond this task without tests. Equating Lord and Baron here means treating their leading tokens as supported syntactic wrappers around the same exact style, not asserting arbitrary titles identify the same person.

In resolution, `PeerageAliases` owns two-stage collection and ambiguity rejection. A useful private intermediate shape is `BTreeMap<PeerageStyle, BTreeSet<PersonalName>>`. Its stable final surface is an observation-ID-to-supported-personal-name map. It can retain bridge provenance internally if needed for diagnostics. It should not expose a mutable alias registry.

## Parsing contract

Accept an explicit bridge only when the entire normalized source consists of one recognized peerage prefix, a name-like short style with exact ` of ` territory, and one terminal balanced parenthetical full personal name. Reject nested, unmatched, multiple, empty, suffix-bearing or role-bearing parentheses. Trim inner whitespace so `(David Sainsbury )` and `(David Sainsbury)` agree. Reuse the same name-word grammar as current personal parsing rather than duplicating its acceptance rules.

Require the parenthetical name to be a full personal name and require its exact surname suffix to agree with the short style's name portion. This grounds the generated full form in the explicit bridge rather than arbitrary parenthetical text. Initials, conjunctions, representative annotations, trading-as text and unexplained parenthetical labels do not create bridges.

For the valid example, the bridge explicitly supports the personal key `david sainsbury`, short style `sainsbury of turville`, and the generated full style `david sainsbury of turville`. Observation matching remains exact after canonical title stripping and normalization. Do not strip arbitrary `of ...` text, match surnames, or construct combinations from unrelated observations.

## Ambiguity and graph safety

Collect every eligible explicit bridge before emitting any key. A style with more than one distinct personal name is ambiguous for the entire run, independent of observation ordering. Emit no peerage evidence from that style, including for its bridge observations and generated full forms. Repeated agreeing bridges remain usable.

Also collect an exact alias-form-to-target set across the surviving bridges. If one supported form maps to different people, exclude that form instead of selecting the first target. A per-observation key must have exactly one target. This prevents a bridge observation from acquiring multiple personal keys and joining distinct people transitively. Include adversarial tests with shared short styles, multiple styles, collisions between a short style and another bridge's full form, and shuffled input order.

Retain the existing exact-name and existing explicit-trading-alias rules. The guarantee here is that the new peerage rule never creates a link without unique supported evidence. If the desired guarantee is stronger, namely that no existing rule can merge an ambiguous style at all, that is a separate semantic policy change and requires explicit review. Exact identical ambiguous source spellings can still match under existing rules, but must not become a conduit to either inferred personal name through this new context.

## Alternatives

A reviewed durable identity registry makes ambiguity and provenance explicit and could capture titles without in-source bridges. It also adds externally maintained identity data, update lifecycle, persistence and review policy. It is structurally sound but larger than this source-contained bug fix and risks person-specific entries.

Full-form inference could derive `david sainsbury` directly from `Lord David Sainsbury of Turville` and match a surname-based short style. It needs no context, but it turns conventional naming structure into identity evidence and cannot safely distinguish territory/name ambiguities or conflicting holders. Reject it for the requested conservative behavior.

The proposed context keeps the parser pure and puts global knowledge in the owner that already holds all observations. This has a smaller public surface than threading alias arrays through cleaning output, stored features, loaders, scorer schemas and proof fixtures.

## Verification and delivery constraints

Parser tests must cover the exact observed source variants, Unicode and punctuation preservation, malformed and role-bearing annotations, unsupported names and matching surname requirements. Resolution behavior tests must include all five observed variants together with plain David Sainsbury, Lord David Sainsbury and Lord (David) Sainsbury, while Francesca Sainsbury and Francesca Perrin remain separate. Add a generic invented-person fixture proving no hardcoded identity.

Prove missing bridge means no new merge, repeated bridge whitespace means one target, conflicting bridges abstain regardless of order, and organisation/unknown-kind/payer/ultimate-payer observations neither supply nor consume peerage evidence. Test no address or low score is required once exact supported evidence exists, while raw scorer names and probabilities remain unchanged.

Test candidate completeness through the actual blocker/scorer path, not only direct calls to classification with manufactured pairs. Verify the known capture through CLI resolve and entity load against an isolated database, then inspect public funder search/detail HTTP responses to demonstrate a single David identity containing the source spellings and separate Francesca identities. Compare occurrence counts and exact GBP totals before and after to establish attribution conservation.

Check formal verification harness imports before implementation. Harnesses that include resolution source files directly will need the canonical funder-name syntax module and its Unicode dependency, or a small compatible module inclusion. Do not copy the parser or title enum into a harness stub, as that proves different behavior. No new stored field is needed because `Observation.name_raw` is already available at the validated resolution boundary.

Scope risk. Adding Baron to the common title vocabulary changes cleaned personal features for Baron names generally. Include focused regression evidence and regenerate any fixtures or digests tied to feature generation. Existing captures can still use the new context because it parses retained raw values; running cleaning again must not be a hidden prerequisite for this repair.
# Proposed design

The caller continues to call `ResolutionInput::new` and `scoring_input`. Input construction derives a peerage evidence index once from validated observations. Blocking and identity classification consult that same index. Raw observations and scorer names stay unchanged.

```rust
// funder_name.rs, syntax and name vocabulary only.
pub enum PersonTitle { /* existing variants */, Baron, Baroness }
impl PersonTitle {
    fn from_token(token: &str) -> Option<Self>;
    fn peerage_style(self) -> Option<PeerageStyle>;
}
pub struct PeerageName { style: PeerageStyle, designation: String }
pub struct PeerageBridge { peerage: PeerageName, personal_name: PersonalName }
impl PeerageBridge {
    pub fn parse(raw: &str) -> Option<Self>;
}
// declaration_resolution/peerage.rs, identity context only.
struct PeerageEvidence {
    names: BTreeMap<FunderObservationId, BTreeSet<PersonalName>>,
}
impl PeerageEvidence {
    fn from_observations(observations: &BTreeMap<FunderObservationId, Observation>) -> Self;
    fn names(&self, id: &FunderObservationId) -> impl Iterator<Item = &PersonalName>;
    fn agrees(&self, left: &FunderObservationId, right: &FunderObservationId) -> bool;
}
```

Treat the sketch as ownership guidance. Avoid introducing a broad public `PersonalName` abstraction if a private normalized string wrapper suffices. Fields stay private so callers cannot fabricate validated bridge evidence. `PeerageEvidence` can remain private to resolution. A public pure bridge parser in funder_name is the only new cross-module capability.

# Grammar and invariants

A valid bridge is precisely one recognized leading peerage title, a nonempty designation, and one terminal balanced parenthetical containing a complete personal name. Trim inside the terminal parentheses, which handles the observed trailing-space variant. Reject nesting, extra parentheses, trailing annotations, conjunctions, digits, role words, and empty or single-token personal names. Reuse the existing alphabetic/apostrophe/hyphen personal-name checks rather than introducing a second policy. Keep capitalization and whitespace normalization identical to existing name features.

Map Lord and Baron into the same masculine peerage style family, and Lady and Baroness only if deliberately supported and tested. Preserve all designation words, including `of`. The key for `Lord Sainsbury of Turville` is the complete normalized designation plus style family. Do not key on surname alone. Do not turn an arbitrary `David Sainsbury of Turville` into `David Sainsbury`.

From the bridge `Baron Sainsbury of Turville (David Sainsbury)`, derive the exact accepted spellings for that bridge: personal `David Sainsbury`, short titled `Lord/Baron Sainsbury of Turville`, and full titled `Lord/Baron David Sainsbury of Turville`. Full form construction is permitted only when the designation's name stem equals the terminal surname of the personal name. Otherwise support the exact short style and personal name without inventing a full form. This restriction prevents blindly inserting personal names into unrelated territorial titles.

Bridge collection is restricted to the existing Individual/Person donor gate. Derive all mappings before resolving any observation. A style key with more than one distinct normalized personal name has no inferred aliases. Keep explicit bridge observations eligible to their own directly asserted personal name only if doing so cannot reattach the ambiguous style through a full form. The simpler conservative policy is to disable all bridge-derived evidence for every observation participating in an ambiguous style, including derived full forms and explicit bridges. Existing unrelated exact-name rules remain as they are.

Prevent bypasses by indexing every bridge and recognized spelling against all identities it could imply before accepting a spelling. An observation spelling recognized under two otherwise unambiguous bridge keys must also abstain. Never implement repeated pairwise rewrites or propagate inferred bridges back into the index. A one-way, two-pass index makes ambiguity independent of observation order and prevents transitive rescue of a conflicted style.

# Integration

`ResolutionInput` adds one private `PeerageEvidence` field populated after existing scope/role checks. Its constructor is the sole production boundary. This avoids changing serialized Observation or persisted cleaning features. Existing raw evidence is sufficient. No migration, SQL changes, load schema changes, or scorer changes are needed.

`blocking_keys` takes the evidence context, or is moved behind a method on ResolutionInput. It emits `individual-donor-name:<personal>` from existing exact person evidence and peerage-derived evidence. Classification receives the same context and accepts intersecting derived personal-name identities only after existing kind conflict checks and both donor/person gates. Retain `ExtractedNameEvidence` as the accepted reason unless provenance requires a dedicated reason. Do not introduce duplicated parsing in blocking and classification.

Exact existing person names must also be represented in the lookup so the explicit bridge reaches stored `David Sainsbury` and its existing title aliases. A new bridge alone does not help if only two derived observations share a new key and the plain personal observation never emits that key. The existing `individual-donor-name` blocking prefix already supplies the desired joining namespace.

The existing component code rejects company-anchor and person/organisation conflicts. It has no person-anchor conflict check. Therefore ambiguity must be resolved before edge creation, across the full dataset, rather than relying on Components to undo unsafe transitive joins. Do not weaken Components or existing address rules.

# Alternatives

A reviewed alias registry would map peerage style to personal identity with review provenance. It is structurally simpler at runtime and strongest against misleading parenthetical source data, but requires a curated artifact, review lifecycle, and likely capture/version semantics. It does not satisfy the evidence-derived generic behavior alone and is a larger product change. Prefer it only if raw source bridges cannot meet an acceptable grammar.

A full-form inference system could pair `Lord David Sainsbury of Turville` with `Lord Sainsbury of Turville` by removing given names, then match `David Sainsbury` by dropping territorial words. Reject it. It invents identity evidence, can merge distinct people sharing a peerage/surname, and its ambiguity boundary is hard to define. The explicit-bridge index retains the same useful paths while requiring source evidence.

Putting all parsing and resolution policy in funder_name would avoid a module but violate its documented purpose as parallel features without identity decisions. Conversely, putting a separate title parser in peerage.rs duplicates PersonTitle vocabulary. Keep syntax and one title vocabulary in funder_name, contextual identity and ambiguity policy in a small resolution module.

# Verification contract

Pure parser tests cover explicit valid bridge, terminal inner whitespace, Unicode names, balanced syntax, rejected roles/nesting/trailing content, and unsupported title formats. Resolution tests use synthetic people and places in addition to the Sainsbury regression. Verify exact short style, bridge variants, derived full form, plain personal name, and existing personal aliases reach one component. Verify Francesca Sainsbury and Francesca Perrin remain distinct, as do same surname/different given name, different territorial designation, organisations, unknown kind, and payer roles.

Ambiguity tests permute observation order and pair order. Include two bridges with one style and different personal names, and two styles whose derived spelling collides. Assert no inferred edge reconnects those identities through bridge or full-form observations. Candidate tests must inspect blocking keys and exercise the actual scorer candidate path at low score. Direct calls to classify alone do not prove completeness.

Formal harness compatibility needs inspection before implementation. Any harness constructing ResolutionInput directly should be migrated to its constructor or a canonical test builder so it cannot omit the context. Prove or exhaustively test that context agreement implies a unique source-supported identity and both observations satisfy the donor/person gate. A bounded harness that stubs the parser can verify graph safety but cannot establish parser correctness; retain ordinary grammar tests.

Capture the real cleaning/resolution CLI before and after against the same isolated snapshot. Compare all affected observation IDs and accepted pair reasons, not only entity counts. Load the resolved artifact into an isolated application database and query public funder/member HTTP endpoints to confirm the intended funder has the combined source occurrences and financial values remain exactly preserved. Verify unrelated funders and total declarations/funding counts remain unchanged. This task changes identity grouping, not amounts or financial selection semantics.

# Synthesis

Choose the source bridge index. It has a small consumer surface, preserves current scorer and persistence contracts, centralizes title parsing, and makes conservative refusal explicit. Its principal review risk is ambiguity laundering through a full-form spelling or the pre-existing exact name rule. Test those paths before adding further heuristics.
# Peerage alias design

## Recommendation

Add a derived, in-memory `PeerageAliasIndex` owned by `ResolutionInput`. Build it once from the complete validated observation set in `ResolutionInput::new`, after duplicate IDs and payment-role references have been checked. Do not persist it in cleaned Parquet, resolved output, or a new table. This is run-local contextual evidence, not a canonical identity declaration. The existing source rows and digest remain the audit record.

The index records only aliases backed by an explicit peerage bridge. Its canonical key is the normalized peerage designation, retaining every designation token such as `of Turville`; its value is the normalized full personal form derived from the bridge. It also indexes the bridge's explicit personal spelling to that same derived full form. A designation with bridges to more than one distinct personal name is ambiguous and contributes no mappings. Repeated equivalent bridges collapse after existing name normalization, including the source's extra inner whitespace.

For the supplied evidence, the one unambiguous bridge is `Baron Sainsbury of Turville (David Sainsbury)`. It establishes `David Sainsbury of Turville`. The parser maps `Lord Sainsbury of Turville`, `Lord David Sainsbury of Turville`, the Baron bridge spelling, and plain `David Sainsbury` to that form. This is an exact designation and explicit-name relation, not a surname or `of` heuristic. Francesca/Perrin remain separate because neither appears in that bridge relation.

## Domain shape and ownership

`funder_name.rs` owns peerage parsing because it already owns `PersonTitle`, normalization, balanced-parenthesis extraction, and evidence-derived name features. Add a peerage-specific parsed form rather than loosening `ParsedPersonName` or stripping titles from arbitrary names. The parsed designation retains the complete normalized tail. The lead token vocabulary is exhaustive and peerage-specific (`Lord`, `Baron`); it must not turn ordinary `lord`/`baron` text elsewhere into a person alias. Validate bridge contents as a simple personal name with the existing personal-name character constraints, and reject unbalanced or multiple-content annotations. Keep the original source spelling intact.

`ResolutionInput` owns the contextual index because it sees the whole run and is already the boundary that validates observations and role references. Suggested private shape:

```rust
struct PeerageAliasIndex {
    by_observation: BTreeMap<FunderObservationId, BTreeSet<PeeragePersonName>>,
}
```

Build a temporary `designation -> BTreeSet<bridge person>` map from eligible bridge observations. Keep only singleton sets. Resolve each eligible observation's parsed peerage designation or exact bridge-person spelling through that map and store the derived alias under its ID. No schema changes are needed. Avoid adding a string field to each observation: doing so would serialize derived contextual state into a source artifact and obscure its provenance.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/peerage_judge
Payload:
Choose **Astra as the base**, with Sol’s explicit warning about collisions across all recognized spellings.

Required refinements:

- Final context must be `observation ID → Option<PersonalName>`, never a set. Each observation gets at most one uniquely supported identity.
- Build ambiguity information from **all bridges before filtering**. Quarantine conflicted styles, their bridge observations, and their generated forms. A surviving bridge must not silently restore a quarantined spelling through a collision.
- Keep the canonical identity `david sainsbury`, as Astra/Sol propose. Luna’s synthesized territorial identity adds unnecessary representation complexity.
- Require a conservative exact `name-stem of territory` bridge grammar and surname agreement before deriving the full form. Reject the whole unsupported bridge rather than introducing Sol’s partial-support branch.
- Preserve existing exact personal-name evidence independently. The new context must abstain on ambiguity without changing established exact-name semantics.

Bound implementation to canonical parsing in `funder_name`, one private resolution context module, constructor initialization, and shared lookups in blocking/classification. Use a separate peerage blocking namespace and index supported ordinary personal observations too. No persisted fields, schema changes, scorer changes, or new public evidence reason are necessary.

Astra has the strongest formal-harness guidance: include the actual canonical parser and dependencies; do not duplicate its vocabulary in stubs. Graft Sol’s adversarial collision tests and Luna’s real CLI-to-loaded-HTTP proof. Acceptance must include missing bridge, conflicting bridges, collision laundering, input-order independence, donor/person gates, untouched raw scoring inputs, and conserved funding occurrences/totals.

## Verification

Rust policy tests cover noncompany identities, exact full-address support, addressless and disagreeing-address donor-name links, mixed evidence, fuzzy and other-role name-only review, sparse-address review, conflicting company anchors, person and organisation conflicts, source-number parsing, reordered input, parent attribution, withholding, and malformed scores. Adapter tests exercise old raw replay, root and nested address isolation, complete Parquet publication, no replacement, and native scorer contracts.

The 43 golden cases in `exposed/tests/fixtures/funder-resolution.json` preserve frozen-model comparison levels and probabilities. They check native parity with the captured scoring behavior, rather than dataset accuracy or calibration.

The Rust integration test `declaration_resolution_cli` creates raw evidence, runs the real `clean` and `resolve` commands with `PATH=/nonexistent`, inspects resulting Parquet rows, and checks input immutability and output refusal. It verifies statistical charity links, Gary Lubner donor links across missing and disagreeing addresses, alias and typed Unite-family links, distinct Carlton Club organizations, and separate Farmer/Sainsbury identities shared by each person's titled, plain, and parenthesized given-name variants. It also checks the observed Sainsbury of Turville short, full, and explicit parenthetical bridges against plain David Sainsbury while retaining separate Francesca Sainsbury and Francesca Sainsbury Perrin identities. No Python installation is needed. Building the CLI still requires an environment that satisfies the existing SQLx macros. See the [resolution guide](../resolution/README.md) for the test command.

The resolved manifest uses schema version 2 for source-only member identities.
Observation and occurrence keys contain numeric Parliament member IDs. Database
member UUIDs never enter resolution artifacts. Loading resolves those source IDs
to the destination database member UUIDs inside the load transaction.

The identity verification crate compiles the canonical peerage context and funder-name syntax, including the shared title vocabulary and Unicode normalization. Existing native fixtures construct that context but contain no explicit peerage bridges. The nine native checks and eleven Kani harnesses retain their existing bounded domains; ordinary application tests cover peerage grammar, ambiguity, and native candidate generation. These proofs do not establish correctness for arbitrary peerage strings.

So this is schema-compatible, but it does affect identity stability and result contents.
